title: Installation & First-Time Configuration
description: Install Git across operating systems and configure identity, default branch names, line endings, and editors.

blocks.content: Before you can start using Git you need to install it and tell it who you are. Every commit you make is stamped with your name and email address - this is how your team knows who made each change.

## Installing Git

Download Git from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com) and follow the installer for your operating system. To check it worked, open a terminal and run:

```
git --version
```

You should see something like `git version 2.45.0`.

## Configuring Your Identity

Run these two commands once after installing. The `--global` flag makes them apply to every project on your machine:

```
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

To check your current settings:

```
git config --global --list
```

## Your Default Editor

Git sometimes opens a text editor (for example, when you write a long commit message). You can set it to something comfortable:

```
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"   # VS Code
git config --global core.editor nano             # nano (simple terminal editor)
```

Installing Git gives your computer the tool. Configuring your name and email puts a return address on every save point you make.

Set this up once, then Git can say who made a change. It does not create an online account or upload your work.

blocks.question: Why do you set your name and email with `git config`?
options: So every commit records who made the change
To unlock push access to remote repositories
Git refuses to work without them
blocks.explanation: Every commit is stamped with the author's name and email. This makes it easy to see who made each change when you look at the project history. It doesn't create accounts or control access by itself.
